scenes.tts: Picture a string of ponds across farmland. Each pond holds a local population, the animals that live and breed there. The fields between are hostile ground. A set of such populations, linked by dispersal, is a metapopulation. Ponds keep losing their populations. Can a region keep a species when no single pond does?
scenes.visual: A string of ponds fills green one by one, hostile ground labelled, dispersal arcs link them, a bracket names the metapopulation, then ponds go grey one by one and a question mark appears.
scenes.narration: Picture a string of ponds across farmland. Each pond holds a local population, the animals that live and breed there. The fields between are hostile ground. scenes.tts: Richard Levins asked this in a simple way. He ignored how many animals each pond holds. Each patch is either occupied or empty. Call the fraction of patches that are occupied p. Occupied patches send out colonists. Colonists can found populations in empty patches. And each occupied patch has some chance of losing its population.
scenes.visual: The ponds become a grid of identical patches, lit if occupied and dark if empty, with a bar for the occupied fraction p. Colonist arrows light an empty patch; one lit patch goes dark.

scenes.tts: Colonization has a rate, called c, per year. It needs colonists from occupied patches, and it works only on empty patches. Extinction has a rate, called e, per year. Each occupied patch loses its population at that rate. Think of a row of lamps that fail at random and get relit from lamps still burning. The row stays partly lit as long as relighting outpaces failure.
scenes.visual: Beside the grid, the Levins equation appears with the colonization term in yellow and the extinction term in red. Patches flash red as they go dark and yellow as they relight.

scenes.tts: Set the change to zero, and the occupied fraction settles at one minus e over c. That is positive only when c is greater than e. Suppose c is zero point four and e is zero point one per year. The fraction settles at zero point seven five. Three patches in four are occupied at any time, though which ones keeps changing.
scenes.visual: A sketch curve of p over years rises from a few occupied patches to a dashed line at 0.75 while the grid fills; then the grid keeps flickering with the same share lit.

scenes.tts: Now let e rise to zero point four, equal to c. The equilibrium falls to zero, and the network is lost. But it is lost slowly. Occupancy starts at zero point seven five and falls by zero point two two five per year at first. After ten years, it is still zero point one nine.
scenes.visual: e changes from 0.1 to 0.4; the dashed equilibrium drops to zero; the sketch curve falls from 0.75 to 0.19 at ten years while the grid thins but keeps lit patches.
scenes.caption: Now let e rise to 0.4, equal to c. The equilibrium falls to zero, and the network is lost. But it is lost slowly. Occupancy starts at 0.75 and falls by 0.225 per year at first. After ten years, it is still 0.19.

scenes.tts: A network at or just past its threshold can keep occupied patches for years, because decline is slowest near the threshold. So seeing animals in some patches does not show that the region is persisting. The model is simple. It assumes identical patches, all equally reachable, with constant rates. Real networks have big and small patches, near and far ones. The rule to keep: a region persists when colonization outpaces local extinction.
scenes.visual: The thinned grid with a question mark; assumption chips appear, then the patches become big and small; finally yellow colonization greater than red extinction labelled persists.
